items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 2 that appeals to longtime residents by calling up their own memories of the station. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Many of us first heard 89.7 as children, crackling through the kitchen radio on snow-day mornings.
options.label: correct
options.why: It draws on a shared, concrete memory that longtime local listeners are likely to have, connecting with their values right before the appeal for money.

options.text: Older listeners may not realize how outdated broadcast radio looks to most people today.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It talks down to the longtime residents the writer hopes will donate and calls the station outdated, which works against the appeal.

options.text: Surveys show that nine out of ten residents rank the station as their favorite local institution.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It brings in a survey nobody can check instead of calling up personal memories, so it does not meet the stated goal.

options.text: Community radio stations across the country have been struggling to pay for equipment lately.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It moves to a national trend and says nothing about local listeners' own memories of 89.7.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3 into a thesis that makes a claim needing proof and previews both body paragraphs (the flood coverage and the station as a town square). Which revision best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The town should give generously, because the station on Kettle Street keeps us informed in a crisis and gives neighbors a place to hear one another.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and names both reasons, emergency information and the town-square role, in the same order as paragraphs 2 and 3.

options.text: Riverbend Community Radio has broadcast from Kettle Street for forty years, through floods, band seasons, and long arguments about rain.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It is a statement of fact that needs no proof, so it does not work as a thesis even though it mentions the topics.

options.text: The town should give generously, because the station on Kettle Street was the only reliable source of news during the March flood.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It previews only the flood paragraph and leaves out the town-square paragraph.

options.text: The town should give generously to every local institution, because small-town media of all kinds are disappearing faster than ever.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It widens the claim beyond the station and does not preview either body paragraph.

items.stem: The writer wants to add commentary after sentence 6 that explains how Hal Pruitt's broadcast supports the claim in sentence 4. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: No playlist could have found a lost dog on Mill Road, because only a voice from Harrow Bend knew which neighbors were asking.
options.label: correct
options.why: It ties the evidence (the local messages Pruitt read) to the claim that streaming services do not know where listeners live.

options.text: Pruitt kept reading message after message for nineteen hours, pausing only for coffee and the weather report.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It adds more detail about the evidence but never explains how that evidence supports sentence 4.

options.text: Pruitt has volunteered at the station since high school and once hosted a popular polka program on weekends.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It gives background on Pruitt and drifts away from the claim instead of linking evidence to reasoning.

options.text: Streaming apps could easily have shared the same flood messages if anyone had thought to upload them that night.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It suggests that streaming could do the same job, which undercuts sentence 4 instead of supporting it.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 9 and 10 into one clear, concise sentence that presents the details in sentence 10 as examples of the claim in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The station is also a kind of town square: on Tuesday nights students discuss their marching band, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall.
options.label: correct
options.why: The colon signals that what follows illustrates the town-square claim, and the sentence is concise and correctly punctuated.

options.text: The station is also a kind of town square because on Tuesday nights students discuss their marching band and on Sundays farmers argue about rainfall.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: 'Because' treats the shows as the cause of the station's being a town square rather than as examples of it.

options.text: The station is also a kind of town square, on Tuesday nights students discuss their marching band, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A comma joins independent clauses, which creates a comma splice.

options.text: The station is also, in a way, a sort of town square, in that on Tuesday nights students talk over band matters and farmers argue about rainfall.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The hedging filler words ('in a way', 'a sort of', 'in that') make it wordy and vague, and it drops the timing of the farmers' show.

items.stem: Some council members have said they worry that dimmer streets would be less safe. The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that addresses this concern while keeping the focus on where the light points. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because shielded fixtures send that wasted light down to the pavement, Cutler Avenue would stay just as bright where walkers and drivers need it.
options.label: correct
options.why: It answers the safety worry directly and ties it to sentence 9's point about misdirected light.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who thinks a dark sky makes streets dangerous has probably never stood in our library lot after sunset.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the council's concern instead of answering it, which would alienate the audience she needs to persuade.

options.text: Shielded fixtures would cut crime on Cutler Avenue by half, making it the safest street in all of Larkhaven within a year.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a sweeping claim about crime with no evidence anywhere in the testimony.

options.text: Many members of our club also enjoy photographing the moon, which looks clearer in a dark sky than under the white globes.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to a hobby detail and never takes up the safety concern.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that gives evidence showing the new Cutler Avenue globes, and not some other cause, are what hid the galaxy. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Last October, when an outage darkened Cutler Avenue for one night, our members found Andromeda from the same lot within minutes.
options.label: correct
options.why: With only the globes removed, the galaxy came back, which isolates the lights as the cause.

options.text: Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away, which makes it one of the most distant objects visible to the eye.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A general astronomy fact about the galaxy; it says nothing about what caused the loss.

options.text: Our club has grown from six members to more than forty, and most of our new members are families from the east side of town.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Club details stay on the topic but give no evidence about what is causing the problem.

options.text: Skies across the whole region have grown brighter for decades as towns and highways have expanded in every direction.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Points to regional growth as a cause, which weakens the claim that the Cutler globes are responsible.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition showing that, after describing the problem in sentence 9, she is now offering proof that it can be solved. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Fortunately, this waste can be fixed:
options.label: correct
options.why: It marks a shift from problem to solution and introduces Fenwick Ridge as proof.

options.text: As a result of this waste,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the sideways light caused Fenwick Ridge's savings, which makes no sense.

options.text: Even so, despite this waste,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals contrast or concession, but sentence 10 builds on the point instead of pushing against it.

options.text: In other words, put simply,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Signals a restatement, but sentence 10 brings in new evidence from another town.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that the two parts of the "not ... but" construction are grammatically parallel. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but that they point the wrong way.
options.label: correct
options.why: Both halves are "that" clauses, so the construction is parallel and the meaning is clear.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but their pointing the wrong way.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Pairs a "that" clause with a gerund phrase, so the halves are still not parallel.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on, but, where they point.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Adds commas that don't belong and still leaves the halves unparallel.

options.text: The problem is not the lights being on but that they are pointed wrongly.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Changes the wording, but it now pairs a noun phrase with a clause and is still not parallel.

items.stem: The details in paragraph 1 suggest that the passage was most immediately prompted by

options.text: a prize announcement that credited authors and publishers while omitting the translators of most of the shortlisted books
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 1-3 describe the Ambervale Prize press release naming six novels, authors and publishers but no translator, though four of the six were translated, including one by the writer.

options.text: a publisher's decision to print the writer's name on an inside page rather than on the cover of a recent paperback
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Sentence 4 mentions the small typeface on page four as a supporting illustration of the problem, but the opening event that occasions the post is the shortlist press release, not a single publisher's layout.

options.text: a jury's refusal to consider novels written in languages that its members are unable to read
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 2 says four shortlisted books were written in languages the jury does not read, so the jury did consider them; the complaint is about credit, not exclusion.

options.text: a reviewer's claim that the prose of a translated novel belonged entirely to its original author
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Reviewers who praise 'the author's luminous prose' appear in sentence 23 as one general cause of invisibility, not as the specific event in paragraph 1 that prompted the passage.

items.stem: In the final sentence of the passage, the writer's reminder to readers who have "ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak" appeals to the audience primarily by

options.text: recasting the demand for credit as a chance for readers to acknowledge a debt they have unknowingly already incurred
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 30 tells readers they 'have already loved a translator's work' and 'simply were not told whom to thank,' turning the request into gratitude readers already owe rather than a new burden.

options.text: warning readers that their admiration for foreign novels has been misdirected toward authors who did not deserve it
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is warm and inclusive, not accusatory; sentence 26 explicitly declines to diminish the author, so the appeal does not suggest authors are undeserving.

options.text: inviting readers to feel superior to reviewers and prize juries who have failed to notice translators
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in sentence 30 sets readers against reviewers or juries; those groups receive their own instructions in sentences 28-29, and readers are addressed on their own terms.

options.text: suggesting that readers who learn foreign languages will no longer need translators at all
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The passage never proposes that readers learn languages; the appeal depends on readers continuing to rely on translations and simply naming those who make them.

items.stem: Taken together, the instructions in paragraph 6 indicate that the writer imagines an audience that

options.text: is made up of fellow translators who need encouragement to abandon their habitual modesty
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Translators are mentioned in sentence 24 as one cause of the problem, but paragraph 6 addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers, not translators.

options.text: includes people in several different roles, each able to change one specific practice
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 28-30 address in turn those who run prizes, those who review books, and readers, assigning each a concrete action, which signals a mixed audience of readers and industry participants.

options.text: consists mainly of publishers who must be persuaded that foreign books are not difficult to sell
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Publishers' fears appear in sentence 22 as a diagnosis, but paragraph 6 does not address publishers directly; its 'If you' clauses name prizes, reviewers and readers.

options.text: shares the writer's expertise and already agrees that translators deserve to be named
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The patient explanation of the plumbing misconception in paragraph 2 and the final reminder that readers 'were not told whom to thank' assume an audience that has not yet considered the issue.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage as a whole?

options.text: Because the English sentences of a translated novel are the translator's own decisions, the translator should be named as the person who wrote them
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 2-3 establish that every English sentence is the translator's choice (sentences 10, 13-15), and paragraph 6 draws the conclusion that a line on the cover should say 'who wrote the English sentences' (sentence 27).

options.text: Because translation changes every sentence of a novel, a translated book is essentially a new work that belongs to the translator rather than the author
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Sentences 18 and 26 explicitly deny this: the writer did not invent the heroine, does not want credit for her, and is not asking for the author's name to be removed or shrunk.

options.text: Because publishers believe that foreign books are difficult to sell, translators will remain invisible until the economics of publishing change
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Publishers' fear is only the first of three causes listed in paragraph 5, and the passage ends with a practical remedy rather than resignation about economics.

options.text: Because translators have cultivated a monkish modesty, they are themselves chiefly responsible for the convention that leaves them unnamed
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Sentence 24 does admit translators' modesty as one cause, but it is one of three 'partly' causes, and the thesis concerns authorship and credit rather than assigning blame to translators.

items.stem: The writer's statement in paragraph 6 that she is "not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound" primarily serves to

options.text: concede that the original author contributes more to a novel than the translator does and therefore deserves a larger share of the credit
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence limits what is being requested; it does not weigh the relative size of contributions, and paragraph 3 has already claimed full authorship of the English sentences.

options.text: forestall the fear that crediting translators would displace authors, so that the request that follows seems modest and easy to grant
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 26 rules out every version of the proposal that might threaten the author's standing before sentence 27 asks only for 'a line of type' the size of a blurb, making the demand hard to refuse.

options.text: acknowledge that publishers' concerns about cover design are legitimate and that translators should accept inside-page credit
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 27 asks for the translator's name 'on the front of the book,' so the writer rejects inside-page credit, which sentence 4 treated with irony.

options.text: introduce a new counterargument about shared authorship that the remaining sentences of the paragraph then refute in detail
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The remaining sentences (27-30) state the proposal and assign actions; they do not refute a counterargument, and the objection about shared credit is dismissed within sentence 26 itself.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents the popular view of translation, and paragraph 3 offers a competing popular view that the writer also rejects
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 3 does not present another popular view; it builds on the writer's own account from paragraph 2 by counting the decisions across a whole novel.

options.text: Paragraph 2 shows a single forced choice in one sentence, and paragraph 3 multiplies that choice across the whole novel to claim its sentences
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 8-10 isolate one decision about 'the weather'; sentence 11 says 'Consider the scale,' and sentences 12-15 multiply roughly forty decisions a page by three hundred pages to conclude 'Every sentence... I wrote.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 argues that translation is impossible, and paragraph 3 reverses course to show that most sentences survive translation intact
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 13 says the English book 'shares none of its sentences' with the Norwegian one, so paragraph 3 intensifies rather than reverses the point that sentences are remade.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes the writer's personal method, and paragraph 3 shifts to statistics gathered from other translators to generalize it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The count in sentence 12 is the writer's own 'rough count' of her own work on Aalvik's novel; no other translators or outside data appear.

items.stem: The question that opens paragraph 5, "Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist?", contributes to the coherence of the passage primarily by

options.text: treating the translator's authorship as settled by the preceding paragraphs and turning the argument toward the causes of a problem
options.label: correct
options.why: The word 'then' in sentence 21 assumes paragraphs 2-4 have established authorship; the question redirects the passage from proving the claim to diagnosing why credit is withheld, which sentences 22-25 answer.

options.text: reopening the objection from paragraph 4 so that the writer can concede that the convention has some justification
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 ends with the rebuttal 'Architecture is credited; so is the building'; sentence 21 does not revive the objection but asks why a practice already shown to be unjust continues.

options.text: signaling that the writer will now abandon personal experience in favor of a survey of publishing history
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 5 still speaks personally ('I confess' in sentence 24) and offers three present-day causes, not a history of publishing.

options.text: introducing the specific remedy that paragraph 6 will later request from prize committees and reviewers
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The question asks for causes, which paragraph 5 supplies; the remedy is introduced only in sentences 26-27 after the diagnosis is complete.

items.stem: The instruction in paragraph 6, "If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release," strengthens the line of reasoning of the passage as a whole chiefly because it

options.text: returns to the specific grievance of the opening paragraph and shows that the general argument yields a concrete fix for it
options.label: correct
options.why: Placeholder

options.text: demonstrates that prize juries, unlike reviewers, are capable of reading the original languages of the novels they judge
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 2 states that the jury does not read the languages of four shortlisted books, so the instruction cannot rest on juries' linguistic ability.

options.text: proves that the three causes enumerated in paragraph 5 can all be eliminated by a single change in prize administration
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Naming translators in press releases addresses prizes only; publishers' fears and reviewers' habits receive separate treatment in sentences 27 and 29.

options.text: shifts the responsibility for translators' invisibility away from the translators who confessed to cultivating modesty
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The instruction assigns a task to prize runners without revisiting the confession in sentence 24; it does not reassign blame, and the passage treats all three causes as jointly operating.

items.stem: In paragraph 1, the detail that the writer's name appears "in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock" chiefly establishes a tone that is

options.text: bitterly indignant, preparing the reader for a direct attack on the publisher's negligence
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence states a measurable fact without any angry adjective, and the passage never attacks a particular publisher; paragraph 2 instead turns calmly to explaining a misconception.

options.text: dryly ironic, letting a factual comparison expose how little the translator's contribution is valued
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 4 makes no complaint outright; ranking the translator's name below the description of paper exposes the absurd priorities of credit through understated comparison.

options.text: resigned and self-deprecating, suggesting the writer accepts that translators rank below physical materials
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage goes on to argue forcefully against this ranking (sentences 14-15, 27), so the detail registers a grievance rather than acceptance of it.

options.text: playfully boastful, hinting that the writer's name will soon become as prominent as the author's
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in sentence 4 predicts future prominence, and sentence 26 explicitly declines any equal or shared billing with the author.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the sentence beginning "But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years" is structured so as to

options.text: accumulate the carpenter's contributions in subordinate clauses before the brief main clause, so the modest conclusion seems earned
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 19 delays its main verb while two relative clauses pile up the carpenter's choices and the client's long residence; the short ending 'is not usually left off the plaque' then lands as an understated, well-supported verdict.

options.text: balance two equal independent clauses so that the carpenter's labor and the architect's design receive matching emphasis
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The sentence has a single main clause with subordinate modifiers; the balanced two-clause structure appears instead in sentence 20, 'Architecture is credited; so is the building.'

options.text: place the main claim first and then qualify it with a list of exceptions in which carpenters do go uncredited
options.label: reversal
options.why: The main claim comes last, not first, and the listed items are the carpenter's contributions supporting credit, not exceptions that withhold it.

options.text: interrupt the argument with a digression about building so that the reader forgets the objection raised earlier in the paragraph
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The carpenter extends the objection's own image from sentence 16 ('a skilled carpenter working from her drawings') in order to answer it, so the structure engages rather than evades the objection.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the writer's overall stance toward Siren on the Ridge?

options.text: Admiration for its reporting combined with a rejection of the conclusion it draws from that reporting
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 calls the reporting 'the book's great strength,' paragraph 3 says 'Where the book falters is in its diagnosis,' and paragraph 6 tells readers to read it for its portraits but 'skeptically when it reaches for the obituary.'

options.text: Gratitude that the book finally documents a crisis, paired with doubt that its figures are accurate
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never questions Weil's numbers; she accepts them as 'the shape of the thing' and disputes only what they mean.

options.text: Respect for its honest portraits, paired with regret that it offers no concrete policy recommendation
options.label: reversal
options.why: Weil does make a recommendation, that counties 'hire paid crews'; the writer objects to that recommendation rather than to its absence.

options.text: Approval of its warning about aging rosters along with a sense that its tone is too sentimental
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The writer praises the volunteers' 'flat, unsentimental voices' and calls the portraits 'honest'; she faults the book's diagnosis, not its emotional register.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's decision to describe the Tillery County levy as 'roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year' is most effective for the intended audience because it

options.text: frames the proposed remedy as a cost small enough that budget-minded officials could adopt it without political risk
options.label: correct
options.why: The passage is aimed at county commissioners who control budgets (sentences 4 and 29); translating the levy into a familiar, modest household expense answers their likely objection about cost.

options.text: reminds commissioners that fuel costs are themselves a major expense in rural fire service
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The tank of gas is a unit of comparison for the levy's size, not a reference to the fire company's fuel costs, which the passage never mentions.

options.text: suggests that households, rather than county boards, should take responsibility for funding equipment
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer's whole argument is that the county, 'not the fish fry,' should buy the truck; the per-household figure describes a public levy, not private donations.

options.text: demonstrates that Tillery County is wealthier than the writer's own county and so can afford more
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage compares the wealth of the two counties; the figure stresses how little the levy costs anyone.

items.stem: The passage can best be understood as a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A newly published book that documents shrinking volunteer rosters and urges counties to replace volunteers with paid crews
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 identifies 'Conrad Weil's new book' as the occasion, and paragraph 3 summarizes its argument that counties should 'hire paid crews.'

options.text: A proposal before the Brannock County board to dissolve the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The dissolved township company is one of Weil's examples; nothing indicates that Marrow Creek faces such a proposal.

options.text: A recent state decision to raise the certified training requirement for new recruits
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The training increase is evidence within paragraph 3, not the occasion for writing; the writer says it rose from forty hours 'when I joined,' not recently.

options.text: The passage of a fire levy in a neighboring county that the writer wants her own county to copy
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The Tillery levy is a counterexample offered as evidence in paragraph 5; the passage opens and closes around Weil's book, not the levy.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the detail that the state 'now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined' is offered primarily as evidence for which claim?

options.text: The volunteer system has been 'quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry'
options.label: correct
options.why: The training detail immediately follows sentence 13 and is the first of two burdens (training, then self-funded equipment) illustrating that claim.

options.text: The volunteer model is 'simply obsolete' because workers no longer live near the station
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is Weil's diagnosis, which the writer is rebutting; the training hours support her counter-explanation, not his.

options.text: 'The people were there all along' but had been 'priced out of serving'
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That claim appears in paragraph 5 and is supported by the Tillery County roster figures, not by the training requirement.

options.text: Weil's reporting is the book's 'great strength' because its figures are so grim
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The training figure comes from the writer's own experience, not from Weil's reporting, and it serves her critique rather than her praise.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer's statement that 'I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire' functions primarily to

options.text: accept the factual basis of Weil's argument in order to isolate and dispute the conclusion he draws from it
options.label: correct
options.why: The concession admits the changed work pattern Weil describes, and the next sentence pivots with 'But obsolete is the wrong word,' narrowing the disagreement to the diagnosis.

options.text: concede that the volunteer model cannot survive and shift the argument toward how paid crews should be funded
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies that the model is obsolete and never endorses paid crews; the concession is limited to the work pattern.

options.text: illustrate with a vivid example how far volunteers now commute, reinforcing Weil's point about distance
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The example is vivid, but its purpose is to set up the rebuttal that follows, not to strengthen Weil's case.

options.text: signal that the writer's own experience is dated and that Weil's more recent reporting should be trusted
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer goes on to cite her own experience of training hours and fundraising as authoritative; nothing suggests she defers to Weil.

items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates how the comparison to 'asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool' in paragraph 4 advances the writer's purpose?

options.text: It transfers a familiar arrangement into a setting where its unfairness is immediately visible, preparing the reader to see fundraising as a structural failure
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 19 says 'The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else,' and sentence 20 then names fundraising 'the structural failure it is'; the analogy makes a normalized burden look absurd.

options.text: It lightens the tone after the grim statistics of paragraph 2, reassuring readers that the crisis is less serious than Weil suggests
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The writer never minimizes the crisis; she calls Weil's warning 'overdue' and uses the analogy to sharpen criticism, not to reassure.

options.text: It provides a second case study that, like Tillery County, shows what happens when public money covers equipment
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The lifeguard is a hypothetical comparison, not evidence; the only case study is Tillery County in paragraph 5.

options.text: It demonstrates that fire companies, like pools, should charge the public user fees for the protection they provide
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The analogy ridicules making the lifeguard raise pool money; it argues against self-funding, not for fees.

items.stem: The sentence 'Where the book falters is in its diagnosis' at the opening of paragraph 3 primarily serves to

options.text: mark the turn from praise to critique while confining the disagreement to Weil's interpretation rather than his facts
options.label: correct
options.why: It follows paragraph 2's praise of the reporting and introduces the critique; the word 'diagnosis' limits the objection to Weil's reading of the evidence, which the rest of the paragraph pursues.

options.text: announce that the writer will now dispute the accuracy of the numbers reported in paragraph 2
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never challenges the figures; she treats them as 'the shape of the thing' and attacks only the conclusion drawn from them.

options.text: summarize the argument of paragraphs 1 and 2 before introducing the Tillery County evidence
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The sentence looks forward to the critique in paragraph 3, not to the evidence in paragraph 5, and it summarizes nothing.

options.text: soften the criticism that follows by acknowledging that every book has minor weaknesses
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is blunt rather than softening, and the flaw it names, the diagnosis, is the book's central argument, not a minor weakness.

items.stem: Paragraph 2 develops its point primarily through

options.text: accumulating specific figures and cases from Weil's reporting to show that the decline is widespread rather than local
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lists the age shift, roster shrinkage, the lone chief, and the dissolved township, then concludes 'These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.'

options.text: contrasting the writer's own department with the departments Weil visited in other states
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer's department does not appear in paragraph 2; the examples all come from Weil's six counties.

options.text: tracing a chain of causes that explains why rosters have aged and shrunk over twenty years
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 2 describes the decline without explaining it; causal explanation begins in paragraph 3 with training and fundraising burdens.

options.text: defining what counts as a functioning fire company and measuring each station against it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No definition or standard is offered; the paragraph relies on reported numbers and portraits.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the sentence 'We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours' emphasizes the writer's point chiefly by

options.text: stacking the roles in a series before the final clause, so that the bewilderment it describes seems unwarranted
options.label: correct
options.why: The four-item list piles up the demands, and the delayed 'and then wondered' lands after the pile, exposing the gap between what was asked and the surprise at the result.

options.text: placing the cause first and the effect last to suggest the loss of volunteers was unforeseeable
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence implies the opposite: given the demands listed, the outcome should have been obvious.

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight to present apathy and overwork as competing explanations
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Apathy is rejected in the previous sentence; this sentence offers a single explanation, not two balanced alternatives.

options.text: repeating the word 'we' to shift blame onto the volunteers themselves for taking on too much
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: 'We' refers to the community and system that made demands, and the blame falls on the burdens imposed, not on the volunteers.

items.stem: In paragraph 1, the semicolon in 'Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three' primarily serves to

options.text: set two matched clauses side by side so the gap between the turnouts conveys how unpredictable a response can be
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins parallel clauses without a connecting word, letting the contrast between nine and three stand starkly and illustrating the 'arithmetic' the writer says Weil understands.

options.text: subordinate the second clause to the first, implying that three responders is the more typical turnout
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A semicolon links independent clauses of equal weight; neither clause is subordinated, and the sentence gives no sense of which turnout is typical.

options.text: introduce an explanation of why fewer volunteers appear on certain nights
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: No explanation follows the semicolon, only a second instance; causes are not discussed until paragraph 3.

options.text: create a pause that signals the writer's shift from personal memory to discussion of the book
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The shift to the book occurs in the next sentence, not at the semicolon, which sits inside a description of turnout.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with an opening that names the class project and the occasion of presenting it to the council's youth advisory panel. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our environmental science class is here to share what nine weeks on the Gannet Road bluffs taught us about how Merrow Point is losing its coast.
options.label: correct
options.why: It names the project, the place and the occasion of reporting to the panel, and it leads straight into sentence 2.

options.text: Coastlines everywhere are changing, and every coastal town faces hard choices about land, money and the sea.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is still a general statement and never mentions the class project or the panel.

options.text: Seawalls have failed Merrow Point, and the council must stop wasting public money on concrete right away.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It opens with an accusation that would put off panel members who support seawalls, and it does not mention the project.

options.text: Beach grass is a hardy plant with deep roots that can hold loose sand in place during heavy winter storms.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It is about one detail from paragraph 3 and does not set up the project or the occasion.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 15 that ends the report by speaking directly to shorefront owners on the panel and connecting the recommendation to their interests. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Planning now gives shorefront owners time to choose how to protect their homes, so they are not left choosing after the next storm.
options.label: correct
options.why: It speaks to the owners' interests and ties planned retreat to protecting their property, which closes the recommendation.

options.text: Shorefront owners who refuse to move will have only themselves to blame when the bluff finally gives way under them.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It blames the very audience the writer needs to persuade.

options.text: Our class also hopes to study water quality in Little Cove next year if the school can find the funding.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It switches to future class plans instead of ending the argument for the council.

options.text: Every shorefront home in Merrow Point will be underwater within ten years unless the council acts this month.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The report's data do not support this exaggerated prediction.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a thesis at the end of paragraph 1 that makes an arguable claim and previews the report's order: the seawall's drawbacks, then the success of dunes and relocation, then the recommendation. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because the seawall has cost the town its beach while dunes and relocation have slowed the losses, Merrow Point should fund those approaches instead of more concrete.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and follows the report's order: seawall, dunes and relocation, recommendation.

options.text: This report describes the seawall, the dunes at Little Cove, the pump station and the lifeguard tower along Gannet Road.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It lists the topics but makes no arguable claim.

options.text: Erosion is a serious problem in Merrow Point, and the town has tried several different ways to deal with it.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Almost no one would dispute it, and it does not preview a line of reasoning.

options.text: Dune restoration and relocation have both failed, so the town should extend the Pell Street seawall north along Gannet Road.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It contradicts the report's evidence and its recommendation.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that explains how the measurements support the claim that dune restoration protects the coast better than the seawall. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Losing a few inches instead of two feet suggests the planted dunes are taking in wave energy that the bare bluff near the wall cannot.
options.label: correct
options.why: It interprets the comparison and links it to the claim that dunes work better.

options.text: We took these measurements with survey stakes on three separate mornings in late October and early November.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It describes the method instead of explaining what the data mean for the claim.

options.text: This proves that dunes will completely stop erosion everywhere along the Merrow Point shoreline for good.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: One season of data at one site cannot show that erosion will stop everywhere.

options.text: The seawall at Pell Street was built in 1998, back when many residents believed walls were the best option.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It goes back over the seawall's history and does not interpret the dune data.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 12 with a transition showing that relocation is a second adaptation the town has adopted alongside dune planting. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Beyond the dunes,
options.label: correct
options.why: It marks relocation as an additional approach, and it does not duplicate the word also already in the sentence.

options.text: As a result of the dunes,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The pump station was not moved because of the dunes.

options.text: In contrast to the dunes,
options.label: reversal
options.why: It treats relocation as opposed to dune planting, but the two are working together.

options.text: Despite the dunes,
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: It suggests the dunes failed and relocation was a reluctant fix.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 9 so its tone is measured and evidence-based for panel members who favor seawalls. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our measurements suggest that dune restoration may protect the coast more effectively than the wall.
options.label: correct
options.why: The hedged, evidence-based wording suits a skeptical audience.

options.text: Dune restoration is obviously the far smarter way to protect the coast, no question.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It is overconfident and dismissive of the audience.

options.text: Dunes are, like, way cooler than ugly concrete walls for protecting stuff.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It is too casual for a report to the council.

options.text: Some people think dunes might possibly help, though honestly nobody can really say.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It hedges so much that it undercuts the report's own evidence.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that readers of the weekly paper who sit on or support the town council will take the comparison as an invitation, not an insult. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our town council, which worked hard last winter on a difficult parking lot decision, might find a useful habit in those Sunday cello sessions.
options.label: correct
options.why: It credits the council's effort and offers the orchestra's habit as a helpful model, so council supporters are not put on the defensive.

options.text: Our town council, which wasted all of last winter bickering over a parking lot, should be embarrassed by a group of amateur musicians.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It is scornful, so it would push away the very readers the writer wants to win over.

options.text: Our town council, which has argued over many issues besides parking for years now, has never once managed to agree on anything at all.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It makes a sweeping charge the column gives no evidence for, and it is also hostile.

options.text: Our town council, which meets on the second Tuesday of each month in the hall, also uses the Grange building for its public hearings.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It gives scheduling trivia and drops the comparison about cooperation altogether.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 3 that would appeal to newspaper readers who think orchestras are only for trained or wealthy people. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Most of them have day jobs, and several borrowed their instruments from the school band closet.
options.label: correct
options.why: It shows ordinary, low-cost membership, which speaks directly to readers who see orchestras as elite.

options.text: Several of them studied at conservatories before they settled in the area to raise families.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It confirms the elite image the writer is trying to correct.

options.text: The program includes two symphonies and an overture that is known for its very hard horn parts.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It describes the music, not who the players are, so it does nothing for these doubtful readers.

options.text: Orchestras have existed in some form for centuries in cities and towns all over the world.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is a general history fact that does not show this orchestra is open to ordinary people.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals it gives more examples of the same kind of cooperation described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: In the same spirit,
options.label: correct
options.why: It marks sentence 10 as more examples of the shared effort in sentence 9.

options.text: On the other hand,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: It signals a contrast, but sentence 10 builds on sentence 9 instead of opposing it.

options.text: As a result of this,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Sentence 9 does not cause the sharing of stands and reeds, so a cause-and-effect link is false.

options.text: Despite these meetings,
options.label: reversal
options.why: It wrongly suggests the sharing goes against the Sunday sessions.

items.stem: The writer wants to add an analogy after sentence 6 that helps general readers see why making room for others, as in this rehearsal, can make one voice heard. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: It was like a dinner table going quiet so the shy cousin at the end can finally finish her story.
options.label: correct
options.why: It matches the move of others getting quieter so one voice can be heard, which is the column's point.

options.text: It was like a coach benching the weakest player so that the stronger players could win the game.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It shows pushing someone out, the opposite of making room for others.

options.text: It was like a car engine running smoothly once every part has been cleaned and well oiled.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It suggests parts working together but leaves out the key idea of stepping back so others are heard.

options.text: It was like a sudden storm passing over Fenwick and then leaving the whole valley bright and calm.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It suggests a change happening by itself, not people choosing to make room.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the details in sentences 9 and 10 support the column's claim that the orchestra works because its players look out for one another. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: None of these habits shows up on the program, yet each one keeps a neighbor ready to play.
options.label: correct
options.why: It ties the unseen habits to players supporting each other, which links the evidence to the claim.

options.text: The cellists also said that their Sunday sessions usually end with coffee and leftover pie.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It adds another detail but no commentary connecting the evidence to the claim.

options.text: Reeds are thin strips of cane that woodwind players need, and they can break very easily.
options.label: off_topic
options.why: It defines a term instead of explaining why the sharing matters for cooperation.

options.text: These habits prove that this orchestra is the finest volunteer ensemble anywhere in the state.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It turns the details into a claim about quality that the evidence cannot support.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace "interesting" in sentence 5's description of the flutes and cellos... rather, wants to revise sentence 5 so that it keeps the warm, lightly humorous tone of a small-town column while still describing the problem. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The flutes were racing for the finish, the cellos were taking the scenic route, and the oboe was lost somewhere in the middle.
options.label: correct
options.why: Its playful, friendly images describe the same problem in a warm, light way.

options.text: The flutes were incompetently rushing, the cellos were sluggishly dragging, and the oboist was an inaudible failure.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It is harsh and mocking toward volunteer neighbors, not warm.

options.text: The flute section exhibited tempo acceleration, the cello section exhibited tempo deceleration, and oboe audibility was insufficient.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Its stiff technical language does not suit a friendly weekly column.

options.text: The flutes, the cellos and the oboe had some problems with the passage that the conductor needed to fix.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is flat and vague, losing both the humor and the specific problem.

items.stem: Taken together, the references to "every bank, hospital, and school district" in paragraph 2 and to "the several thousand of us who were standing on her work" in paragraph 6 suggest that the writer imagines her audience primarily as

options.text: people who benefit from volunteer-maintained code without having recognized that dependence
options.label: correct
options.why: The institutions named in paragraph 2 are those that unknowingly run code on hidden walls, and the closing sentence counts the reader among the thousands who failed to notice they were standing on the schoolteacher's work.

options.text: volunteer maintainers who have themselves considered deleting projects after abusive bug reports
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The writer is a former maintainer, but she addresses the dependent many, not the lone maintainers; the closing sentence places readers among those standing on the work, not among those doing it.

options.text: corporate executives who already fund open-source foundations and want their money spent well
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Sponsoring foundations are Alcock's proposed remedy, which the writer rejects; nothing frames the reader as an existing sponsor.

options.text: readers of Alcock's book who have already accepted his argument and need to be talked out of it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 6 tells readers to read the book, implying they have not yet; the writer anticipates rather than corrects their response.

items.stem: The comparison to volunteer fire departments in paragraph 5 is most likely intended to appeal to the audience's

options.text: belief that people exposed to a shared danger owe one another participation rather than payment
options.label: correct
options.why: The analogy stresses that the people whose houses would burn show up for drills instead of mailing a check, modeling the claim that obligation should attach to dependence and be paid in hours.

options.text: admiration for individuals who continue dangerous unpaid work out of personal stubbornness
options.label: reversal
options.why: The analogy rejects reliance on the one person who owns a hose; stubborn individuals are what the writer wants to stop depending on.

options.text: distrust of small towns that neglect essential services until an emergency forces action
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The fire department is presented as a successful model, not as an example of neglect.

options.text: assumption that institutions with ninety engineers can easily afford modest sponsorship stipends
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The bank example concerns a failure to assign hours, and the fire department analogy argues against checks, not for affordable ones.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences from the passage most directly states the writer's central claim?

options.text: "The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars."
options.label: correct
options.why: This sentence states the writer's own prescription, which the whole review builds toward and which the closing return to the schoolteacher restates.

options.text: "The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: This endorses only the diagnosis; the review's distinctive claim concerns the cure, which this sentence does not address.

options.text: "Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This is the rebuttal of Alcock's remedy, a supporting step, but it does not state what the writer proposes instead.

options.text: "Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get."
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: This is the reviewer's verdict on the book's merit, not the argumentative claim about where maintenance obligation lies.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence beginning "This will not rescue every project" primarily serves to

options.text: limit the reach of the proposal so that it cannot be dismissed for failing to solve every case
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer concedes that the smallest libraries will still depend on individuals, then reasserts the proposal's main benefit of spreading the weight; the qualification preempts an objection.

options.text: concede that Alcock's sponsorship model remains necessary for the smallest and most neglected libraries
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sentence says small libraries will rely on individual stubbornness; it does not reintroduce sponsorship as a fallback.

options.text: signal that the writer has come to doubt whether institutions will contribute hours at all
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence ends with a confident claim that the proposal would spread the weight; it qualifies scope, not conviction.

options.text: return to the load-bearing metaphor in order to restate the diagnosis offered in paragraph 2
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The sentence does reuse the wall image, but its purpose is to bound and defend the cure, not to restate the diagnosis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage's overall thesis is organized?

options.text: An endorsement of the book's diagnosis, a rejection of its proposed cure, and a substitute remedy
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 praises the diagnosis, paragraphs 3 and 4 reject sponsorship, paragraph 5 offers hours instead of dollars, and paragraph 6 compresses this into read the first half, argue with the second.

options.text: A summary of the book's evidence, a defense of its conclusions, and a call for a wider readership
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer disputes rather than defends the book's conclusions about the cure; only the diagnosis is accepted.

options.text: A personal account of maintaining software, a critique of corporate funders, and a plea for gratitude
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The personal account supports the argument but is not its spine, and the proposal concerns assigned hours, not gratitude from users.

options.text: A description of the tidyclock outage, an analysis of its causes, and a prediction that it will recur
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The outage frames the review, but the passage argues about remedies rather than predicting repetition.

items.stem: The writer's assertion in paragraph 5 that the better cure is "visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it" is most effective at

options.text: presenting her alternative as consistent with Alcock's own evidence rather than as a rejection of his project
options.label: correct
options.why: By locating the cure inside the book, the writer frames her disagreement as completing Alcock's work with his own material, which keeps her praise of the first half credible.

options.text: suggesting that Alcock deliberately suppressed a conclusion that would have displeased corporate sponsors
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage attributes motive or suppression to Alcock; the writer calls his faith in a check puzzling, not dishonest.

options.text: conceding that her proposal is less original than Alcock's and therefore less likely to be adopted
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Locating the cure in his margins does not weaken her proposal; the writer calls it the better cure and argues for it confidently.

options.text: retracting her earlier judgment that the second half of the book loses its footing
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence introduces the alternative to Alcock's cure; it sustains, rather than withdraws, the criticism of the second half.

items.stem: The writer's use of the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway in paragraph 3 primarily advances her purpose by

options.text: rendering an abstract claim about payment and obligation in a scene readers can test against their own experience
options.label: correct
options.why: The analogy makes concrete the claim that a stipend changes what the work is, showing how paying converts a gift into a service and gives the payer the right to complain.

options.text: supplying a documented case in which sponsorship caused a volunteer to abandon a project
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The neighbor is a hypothetical illustration, not a documented case, and the neighbor does not quit; the point is the changed relationship.

options.text: proving that maintainers would refuse payment if it were offered to them
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The analogy says nothing about refusal; the writer even grants that stipends have saved projects.

options.text: contrasting neighborly generosity with the hostility of the bug reports described in paragraph 4
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The analogy is about what payment does to a gift, and it precedes the bug report testimony rather than contrasting with it.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer develops the claim that institutions "lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do" chiefly through

options.text: a hypothetical example of a single institution followed by a comparison to a familiar civic practice
options.label: correct
options.why: The regional bank with ninety engineers illustrates the missing sense of ownership, and the volunteer fire department supplies the model of what ownership looks like.

options.text: a sequence of causes tracing how convenient downloads accumulated into a fragile structure
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That causal account of accretion appears in paragraph 2, not in the development of paragraph 5.

options.text: a survey statistic showing how few engineers at dependent firms review open issues
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The only survey statistic is Alcock's in paragraph 2 about packages, and the bank example gives no survey figure about engineers.

options.text: a personal anecdote about a bank that once ignored her requests for assistance
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The bank is a generic illustration of a login page running tidyclock, not an episode from the writer's own history.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the clause "the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice" chiefly emphasizes

options.text: how a single act of payment sets off a chain of consequences that ends with the payer entitled to complain
options.label: correct
options.why: The introductory time clause marks the one triggering moment, and the three parallel main clauses accumulate consequences, with the final one landing on the payer's new entitlement.

options.text: how the neighbor's labor grows heavier with each winter that she is left to shovel alone
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The clauses describe changes in the relationship after payment, not increasing physical labor over years.

options.text: how a service, a problem, and a right are three separate benefits the neighbor gains from being paid
options.label: reversal
options.why: Only the last clause names a right, and it belongs to the payer, not the neighbor; the series records losses of the gift character, not benefits.

options.text: how uncertain it is whether the neighbor will continue shoveling once money is involved
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The parallel declaratives are flatly certain; nothing in the structure conveys doubt about continuation.

items.stem: The writer's choice of the first-person plural in "owed us nothing" in paragraph 2 and "the several thousand of us" in paragraph 6 is most effective because it

options.text: places the writer alongside her readers among those responsible, so the proposal reads as shared duty rather than accusation
options.label: correct
options.why: By counting herself among the dependents who failed to notice, the writer turns the final charge into a collective admission, which suits an argument that obligation attaches to dependence.

options.text: separates the writer and other maintainers from the institutions that profit from their unpaid labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: The pronoun includes the writer with the dependents who were standing on the work, not with the maintainers set apart from them.

options.text: directs the closing sentences specifically at Alcock as the one reader most in need of correction
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The plural widens the address to everyone who ran code on the walls; Alcock is not singled out in these sentences.

options.text: softens the review's criticism by implying that the writer herself once favored corporate sponsorship
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing suggests the writer ever favored sponsorship; the shared failing is not noticing dependence, not endorsing a check.

items.stem: The details in paragraph 1 suggest that the passage is most directly a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A local institution has circulated a pledge whose practice the writer supports but whose wording she believes misplaces responsibility.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 3 names the exact unease: she agrees with the proposal and distrusts its wording, and sentences 4 and 5 question who took the table from the children.

options.text: A local institution has asked households to give up their devices entirely, a demand the writer considers unrealistic for modern families.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The card asks only for screens down at supper (sentence 2); nothing in the passage indicates a demand to abandon devices, and the writer later praises keeping machines (sentence 16).

options.text: A reader of the magazine has argued publicly that the writer's own family history offers no guidance for households today.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No challenge from a reader appears; the occasion is the arrival of the pledge card in the library's envelope (sentence 1).

options.text: A library newsletter has reported that children in the town are spending more hours on screens than their parents did at the same age.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The newsletter is mentioned only as the envelope's other contents (sentence 1); no report or comparison of children's screen hours is given anywhere in the passage.

items.stem: Taken together, paragraphs 3 and 6 best convey which of the following as the writer's stance toward new household machines?

options.text: They are intrusions that a careful household should keep out of the home as long as it reasonably can.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 15 states the household did not bar the stranger, and sentence 16 notes each machine stayed; the writer never recommends keeping machines out.

options.text: They are welcome once the household, adults included, decides when they may and may not have its attention.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 15 through 17 describe telling the stranger when to call and marking off one hour, and sentence 30 directs the adult reader to put the phone in the drawer for that hour.

options.text: They are tolerable for adults, who can regulate themselves, but harmful to children until they learn restraint.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage repeatedly locates the problem with adults (sentences 9, 14, 29, 30), not with children who must learn restraint.

options.text: They are each less disruptive than the one before, so households now have little reason to regulate them.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer presents the pattern as recurring and still necessary (sentences 12, 32, 33); she never ranks machines by disruptiveness or suggests regulation is now unneeded.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the writer's inclusion of the radio's price, "thirty-one dollars and forty cents," as recorded in the ledger primarily functions to

options.text: establish that the family's hardship, not the grandfather's habits, explains why the radio was restricted at meals
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The passage attributes the rule to the grandfather's behavior (sentence 9), not to cost; the price is never linked to the reason for the restriction.

options.text: lend documentary precision to a family story that might otherwise seem like fond invention
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 6 ties the exact figure to a ledger kept in the grandmother's hand, and sentences 7 and 8 continue to cite the ledger as a record, grounding the anecdote in a written source.

options.text: signal that the writer has verified the ledger's figures against other historical records of the period
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer cites only the household ledger (sentence 6); no outside verification or comparison with other records is mentioned.

options.text: suggest that the family valued the radio too highly to have ever considered removing it from the house
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The price is offered as a ledger detail, not as an explanation of attachment; the decision to keep rather than bar machines is argued separately in sentence 15.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences from the passage most fully states the writer's central claim?

options.text: "The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Sentence 12 introduces the enumeration in paragraph 3 and asserts repetition, but it says nothing about the curfew-versus-ritual distinction that the essay builds toward.

options.text: "There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen."
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 18 names the distinction that reinterprets the anecdotes of paragraphs 2 and 3, anchors the concession in paragraph 5, and drives the instruction to cross out the second line in paragraph 6.

options.text: "Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Sentence 25 is the narrowing move within the concession; it qualifies a supporting point rather than stating the governing argument about shared ritual.

options.text: "My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford."
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Sentence 31 is a closing gesture that refers back to the claim with the pronoun 'this'; it depends on earlier sentences and does not itself state the claim.

items.stem: The 1967 ledger entry quoted in paragraph 3, "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included," most directly serves as evidence for the claim that

options.text: the household's rules grew stricter with each new machine as the children became teenagers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing indicates escalating strictness; the passage stresses that the household did 'the same thing' each time (sentence 15).

options.text: the grandmother's rule had failed by the next generation and had to be written down again from scratch
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentence 12 frames the new entry as the pattern repeating, a continuity rather than a failure; the writer treats the repetition as instructive, not as a collapse.

options.text: the family's supper rule, across generations, bound the adults of the household as explicitly as it bound the young
options.label: correct
options.why: The quoted phrase 'Dad included' echoes sentence 11, where the grandmother built the fence to keep herself and her husband inside, showing the rule's application to adults persisted into 1967.

options.text: television proved more tempting to the family than the radio or telephone had been
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage does not compare the pull of the machines; the entry names the father, paralleling the radio story (sentence 9), rather than ranking devices.

items.stem: The two questions that close paragraph 1, "Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?", prepare the reader for the rest of the passage primarily by

options.text: announcing that the writer will refuse the pledge and explain her refusal through family history
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer signs the card (sentence 28); her unease is with the wording, not the proposal (sentence 3).

options.text: posing a question of responsibility that the family narrative then answers by pointing to the adults
options.label: correct
options.why: The question of who took the table is answered in sentence 9 (the grandfather was the trouble), sentence 14 ('Dad included'), and sentence 29 ('Do not give the children back the table').

options.text: establishing a playful tone that the writer sustains through the historical paragraphs and the closing appeal
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone shifts to wry narration, then candid concession, then assured exhortation (sentences 12, 23, 28); the questions voice unease, not sustained play.

options.text: introducing the distinction between curfew and ritual that paragraph 4 will define in detail
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The questions concern who is responsible for leaving the table; the curfew-versus-ritual distinction is a separate conceptual move introduced only in sentence 18.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents a single founding example, and paragraph 3 shows that the household's response recurred with each later machine.
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 12 opens paragraph 3 with 'The pattern repeated itself,' and sentences 13 through 16 enumerate the telephone and television following the same scheduling response established in sentences 8 through 11.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes a rule that worked, and paragraph 3 explains why later generations found it impossible to maintain.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 3 shows the rule being renewed, not abandoned; the 1967 ledger entry repeats the grandmother's rule (sentence 14).

options.text: Paragraph 2 relies on family memory, and paragraph 3 corrects that memory with written records from the ledgers.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Both paragraphs draw on ledgers and memory alike (sentences 6, 8, 9, 13, 14); paragraph 3 does not correct paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 2 narrates the grandmother's rule, and paragraph 3 defines the terms that make the rule a ritual rather than a curfew.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The definitions of curfew and ritual belong to paragraph 4 (sentences 18 through 20); paragraph 3 extends the narrative pattern rather than defining terms.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing" is most logically effective because it

options.text: withdraws the preceding concession and reasserts that the quiet hour did in fact produce conversation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never retracts the admission; sentence 25 grants that the hour produced only attendance, and sentence 27 continues to describe the suppers as sullen.

options.text: accepts the narrowed claim of the previous sentence and then asserts that the narrowed claim still carries weight
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 25 reduces the hour's benefit to attendance; sentence 26 accepts that reduction with 'But' and 'not nothing,' and sentence 27 supplies the memory evidence that attendance is what endured.

options.text: introduces new ledger evidence that contradicts the letters describing sullen, silent meals
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No new ledger evidence appears; sentence 27 offers the mother's memory, which confirms rather than contradicts that the suppers were sullen.

options.text: shifts the argument from the family's history to the reader's household before the final paragraph begins
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The turn to the reader occurs in sentence 28 with 'I would urge you'; sentence 26 remains within the evaluation of the family's recorded suppers.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the structure of the sentence "Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect" emphasizes the relationship between ideas by

options.text: opening with a dependent clause that states the goal, so that the commands which follow appear as mere suggestions
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The sentence begins with imperatives ('Sit down,' 'let them see you'), not with a dependent clause; the 'until' clause is placed last.

options.text: placing a series of imperatives first and the "until" clause last, so that the actions lead toward an end point in which the rule's original target is forgotten
options.label: correct
options.why: The commands come first, with the interrupting phrases 'phone in the drawer' and 'every night,' and the final subordinate clause names the outcome: shared ownership and no memory of whom it protected, which answers paragraph 1's question.

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight, so that the parent's action and the child's observation appear as separate obligations
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are coordinated imperatives aimed at the same adult reader, and the child's role is to see the adult; nothing presents the child as bearing an obligation.

options.text: repeating the word "you" at the start of each clause, so that the reader is singled out as the person the pledge was designed to protect
options.label: reversal
options.why: 'You' is not clause-initial, and the sentence ends by saying nobody remembers whom the rule protected; the reader is addressed as the adult who must comply, not as the protected party.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the colon in the sentence "By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: 'No set from six to seven. All of us.'" is most effective because it

options.text: holds back the ledger's words until the contrast between a sum and a sentence has been set up, giving the handwritten rule the weight of a quoted document
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon builds expectation by noting the entry is 'not a sum but a sentence,' and the colon then presents the rule itself, which the essay later treats as its key text (sentence 22, 'All of us').

options.text: separates the writer's own commentary on the rule from the grandmother's words so that readers can judge the rule without the writer's interpretation
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The material before the colon is description of the ledger, not commentary on the rule; interpretation comes afterward in sentences 10 and 11, not before.

options.text: signals that the ledger entry was written hastily, in the moment of frustration with the grandfather's listening
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing about the punctuation or the surrounding text suggests haste; the entry appears five days after the purchase (sentences 7 and 8), and the grandfather's behavior is explained only in sentence 9.

options.text: joins two independent statements about the purchase so that the Tuesday entry and the Sunday entry read as a single financial record
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The colon introduces a quotation, not a second independent clause, and the Sunday entry is explicitly 'not a sum,' distinguishing it from the financial record of the purchase.
